Volume 17 · Chapter 06

Grading, feedback and remediation

Professional Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v17-c05

By the endGrade consistently and give feedback that identifies the next learning action.

A useful grade identifies what the work demonstrates. Useful feedback tells the learner what to do next—and what new evidence will show whether that action worked.

Capability. Apply an explicit rubric consistently, adjudicate disagreements using the submitted reasoning, and design targeted correction followed by fresh reassessment. The prerequisite is problem design and meaningful assessment. We reuse dated present value and the two-group difference-in-differences identity, restating the necessary mathematics. Every response, grade and classroom exchange below is an original synthetic specimen. No real student record, implemented course or measured grading reliability is asserted.

1. Separate the score, the diagnosis and the next decision

A criterion names a feature of the intended performance. An analytic rubric separates that performance into components with explicit evidence and points. A score records the demonstrated components under those rules. A diagnosis is a provisional explanation of an error; it may need a short follow-up question. Remediation is targeted practice addressing that explanation. Reassessment elicits new evidence under stated conditions, rather than merely checking whether the learner copied the supplied correction.

For criterion j, let mj be its maximum and sj the awarded points, with 0≤sj≤mj. The task percentage is 100Σsj/Σmj, requiring a positive total maximum. Addition is straightforward; deciding whether a response satisfies a descriptor requires disciplinary judgment. A correct conclusion reached through an invalid assumption is different from a correct method with one multiplication slip. Record the particular evidence supporting the points and the particular missing capability. Do not infer a person's ability or intent from a single mark.

Carnegie Mellon describes rubrics as component-specific expectations that can support grading and formative feedback.[1] Cornell recommends concrete performance descriptors and feedback on the rubric itself before revision.[2] Those are design recommendations. They do not validate our point allocations, demonstrate that every grader will agree, or guarantee learning gains.

Carry-forward credit means awarding a later, separately assessable step when it is correctly performed using an earlier erroneous quantity. It is appropriate only when that step still demonstrates the intended skill. A two-unit valuation slip need not erase evidence of a correctly dated financing reconciliation. But inventing a counterfactual trend and then drawing a causal conclusion is not evidence of valid identification. Specify the policy before grading: where will the original error be charged, and what later reasoning remains meaningful? Never award the same evidence twice under overlapping criteria.

Maintain a separate critical-repair flag for an unfunded decision, unsupported causal claim or unsupported evidence assertion. A high aggregate score does not clear that flag. Our proposed progression rule is at least 85% overall, at least 75% in each essential domain and resolved critical errors, followed by independent transfer. It is an internal teaching choice, not an institution's policy or a calibrated guarantee. An academic-integrity concern additionally requires evidence and the actual institution's process; a grader must not silently convert an unsupported sentence into a finding of deliberate misconduct.

2. Calibrate judgments, not just totals

Calibration is the process of making graders' interpretations comparable. Before general marking, select a small set of responses spanning clear success, an arithmetic slip, a conceptual error and an ambiguous argument. Have graders score them independently using the same rubric version. Compare criterion vectors and cited passages, then write an adjudication explaining which descriptor applies. A negotiated average can conceal a disagreement about what the learner actually demonstrated. If the key or descriptor is defective, repair it and revisit every affected submission, including those whose authors did not appeal.

Carnegie Mellon's grading guidance recommends discussing sample work and rubric interpretation, examining reasoning, and considering which language or presentation features actually belong to the learning objective.[3] Our implementation is to record a rubric version, the original scores, the disputed evidence, the resolution and the set needing regrading. Where feasible, obscure irrelevant identity information and grade the same question across responses. Neither step establishes that all bias has disappeared.

For n double-scored scripts, define the signed mean difference B=(1/n)Σ(aᵢ−bᵢ), mean absolute difference A=(1/n)Σ|aᵢ−bᵢ|, and exact agreement E=(number with aᵢ=bᵢ)/n. All require n>0. B=0 can coexist with substantial disagreement because positive and negative differences cancel. Even E=1 on a few examples does not prove reliability on future tasks. Use these descriptive summaries to locate work for inspection; do not advertise them as a validated reliability coefficient. A rubric can also be consistently wrong if all graders apply an invalid key.

3. Worked grading packet: preserve the method and repair the error

Case 1 — Dated value, a reserve and carried arithmetic

Complete assignment. A project has (cost now, certain year-1 receipt, certain year-2 receipt)=(64,50,50) currency units. The annual discount rate is 1/4. Opening cash and the immediate minimum reserve are (90,30). There are no taxes, other costs or subsequent reserve commitments. Doing nothing has value zero. First assess the project without borrowing. Then a permitted loan supplies 4 now and requires 5 at year 1, with no other fee: (4,5). Label the dates, calculate NPV, check the reserve in each regime, reconcile the financed equity cash flows and recommend a feasible choice. Use the same discount rate for all stipulated certain flows. Show reasoning; merely naming a choice is insufficient.

Instructor solution. At times 0,1,2 the project flows are (−64,50,50). Discounting reverses compounding, so the receipts are worth 50/(5/4)=40 and 50/(5/4)²=32 now. The NPV is −64+40+32=8. The checked vector (first PV, second PV, NPV) is (40,32,8). Without borrowing, cash is 90−64=26<30, so a positive-value project is nevertheless infeasible. With the permitted loan cash is 90+4−64=30, exactly meeting the immediate reserve.

The equity flows become (-60,45,50); their value is −60+45/(5/4)+50/(5/4)²=8. The loan has NPV 4−5/(5/4)=0. More generally, at a common per-period rate r>−1, adding dated project and financing flows adds their NPVs because each common-date discount sum distributes over addition: Σ(Pₜ+Fₜ)/(1+r)ᵗ=ΣPₜ/(1+r)ᵗ+ΣFₜ/(1+r)ᵗ. Here Pₜ and Fₜ are the two signed cash flows at the same date t. Zero financing value here follows specifically from the matched rate and absence of fees. The cash/value results are (26,30,8,0). Choose the outside option without borrowing, and the financed project with this loan; those statements depend on the supplied objective and constraints. Later receipts do not pay an immediate reserve requirement.

Published analytic rubric: twenty points; criterion order used in the score vectors
CriterionMaximumEvidence and partial-credit rule
F1: labeled timeline21 for cost labeled at date 0; 1 for both receipts labeled at dates 1 and 2. No date labels earns neither point.
F2: discount setup42 for the first receipt's correct rate/exponent; 2 for the second's. A missing or wrong denominator earns zero for that receipt.
F3: numerical valuation41 for first correct discounted receipt; 1 for second; 2 for correct subtraction/addition of the learner's explicitly reported receipt values and cost. Carry the receipt error into this last operation without a second deduction.
F4: cash accounts42 for correct immediate cash without borrowing; 2 for correct immediate cash with borrowing. Assess the decision separately in F6.
F5: financing reconciliation42 for all three correctly dated equity flows; 2 for consistently reconciling their discounted value to project value plus loan value. Carry an earlier numerical PV slip, but do not excuse a missing repayment or wrong date.
F6: conditional choice21 for choosing the outside option when the reserve fails; 1 for the financed positive-value choice conditional on the stated terms. Correct implications of carried values retain credit; an unfunded recommendation does not.

Synthetic response N, reproduced in full. “Date 0 costs 64; dates 1 and 2 pay 50 each. PV₁=50/1.25=40; PV₂=50/1.25²=30. NPV=−64+40+30=6. No loan leaves 26, below 30, so do nothing. The loan leaves 30. Equity payments are −60 now, 45 in year 1, 50 in year 2. Their value is −60+36+30=6, the same as project value because 4−5/1.25=0. With that loan choose the project; the reserve is only immediate and these are the stated certain flows.”

Grade and adjudication. N supplies the correct second-year denominator but evaluates it incorrectly. The vector (2,4,3,4,4,2) totals 19 out of 20. F3 loses its second-receipt point; N combines the reported numbers correctly. F5 still demonstrates the financing decomposition. Suppose grader A initially gives F5 only 2 because the final equity NPV is also wrong, yielding 17, while grader B gives 19. The published carry-forward rule resolves this to 19, not the average 18. The corrected amount remains compulsory feedback; partial credit does not make 30 the right present value.

Feedback to N. “Your dates, discount denominators and reserve decisions are sound. Recalculate the second present value: multiply your 30 by 1.25² and compare it with the promised 50. Replace that value in both reconciliations and explain why the loan still contributes zero NPV. Then solve the new task below without the worked solution. The immediate objective is an inverse-compounding check, not repeating all of finance.” The repair computation is 30×25/16=46.875 rather than 50; 32×25/16=50. The corrected project and equity NPVs are both 8. These are checks on the submitted work, not proof that N has a stable misconception.

Synthetic response K, reproduced in full. “The NPV is 50+50−64=36, so buy. Cash is 90−64=26, which is fine because the future receipts will cover the reserve. There is no reason to consider the loan.” K supplies no labeled timeline or discount denominator. The vector (0,0,2,2,0,0) totals 4. F3 awards the internally correct addition/subtraction of the stated amounts, not correct present valuation; F4 awards only the unfinanced cash account. The unfunded choice sets a critical-repair flag.

Feedback and repair for K. “Your 26 is the correct immediate cash, but it violates the required 30. Place the cost and both receipts on a three-date line. Mark which cash is available at the instant the reserve is checked; explain why year-1 money cannot enter that instant without a permitted contract. Next discount each receipt separately and compare the two borrowing regimes.” A complete repair says: “At date 0, 90−64=26 fails. The future receipts arrive at dates 1 and 2, whose PVs are 40 and 32, giving NPV 8. With 4 borrowed now, date-0 cash becomes 30 and the repayment changes year-1 equity receipts to 45. The financed value is still 8.” A copied correction is practice evidence, not clearance of the critical flag.

Fresh reassessment and complete key. Independently analyze a different project with cost 54 now and receipts 36 at each of years 1 and 2, at rate 20%; opening cash 80, immediate reserve 30; permitted loan 4 now repaid 4.8 at year 1. Inputs are (54,36,36,1/5,80,30,4,24/5). Use the same six criteria, with the new amounts. Receipt PVs are 30 and 25; NPV is 1. No loan leaves 26 and fails; borrowing leaves 30. Equity flows are (−50,31.2,36), with NPV −50+26+25=1. Thus (30,25,1,26,30,-50,31.2,36,1). The loan value is zero. Choose no project without financing, and the financed project under these terms. An evaluator also asks what happens if the reserve rises to 31: the offered loan is insufficient. Score the actual new response and check the critical decision; do not pre-record that N or K passed merely because a key exists.

4. Worked grading packet: a correct contrast does not establish a cause

Case 2 — Evidence claims, assumptions and a correction memo

Complete assignment. A fictional program starts between two dates in group T, while C is the comparison group. The table contains observed participation percentages. There is no randomization claim, participant-level data, sample-size information, standard error or assignment/sampling law. Calculate each change and their difference, explain conditions needed for causal interpretation, state what statistical significance can be concluded, and write a short recommendation for further evaluation. Do not invent observations.

Supplied rates, in percent; changes are percentage points
GroupBeforeAfter
T4055
C3037

Instructor derivation. T rises 15 percentage points, C rises 7, and D=(55−40)−(37−30)=8 percentage points: (15,7,8). This is not an 8% proportional increase. For a fixed target population with a consistent outcome definition, let τ be the mean post-program effect on T, and let δ be T's untreated change minus C's untreated change. With an unaffected baseline, no spillovers into the comparison, and consistent observation of these groups, add and subtract T's untreated post mean. To see every term, write T₀,T₁,C₀,C₁ for the four observed means and U₁ for T’s untreated post mean. Then D=(T₁−T₀)−(C₁−C₀)=(T₁−U₁)+[(U₁−T₀)−(C₁−C₀)]=τ+δ, hence τ=D−δ. Parallel untreated trends sets δ=0; a level difference at baseline need not be zero. No arithmetic operation on these four observed rates establishes δ=0.

For a concrete proof of non-identification, keep the observed table unchanged. World A sets T's unobserved untreated post mean to 47: its untreated change equals C's 7, so (τ,δ)=(8,0). World B sets that untreated mean to 55: its untreated change is 15, so (τ,δ)=(0,8). All means are inside [0,100]. The observed rates fit both worlds, (47,8,0,55,0,8) in the order (untreated T after, effect, trend gap) for each. The table therefore does not choose between a positive effect and no effect. With no uncertainty model or supporting data, it also supplies no justified p-value.

Published evidence rubric: twenty points
CriterionMaximumEvidence and partial-credit rule
E1: observed changes42 for each correct group change stated in percentage points.
E2: contrast42 for subtracting comparison change from target change; 2 for the correct resulting contrast. Correct carried subtraction can earn the method points.
E3: identification62 for the parallel untreated-trend restriction; 2 for stable group composition and comparable outcome measurement; 2 for an unaffected baseline and clean comparison, including no anticipation or relevant spillovers. State conditions, not proof that the data satisfy them.
E4: uncertainty22 for stating that no justified significance calculation is available from the supplied information; zero for an invented p-value or unsupported significance claim.
E5: bounded recommendation42 for a conclusion clearly limited to the observed contrast or to explicitly conditional causal assumptions; 2 for a concrete next evidence step connected to an identification or inference limitation. Unsupported universal adoption earns neither.

Synthetic response P, reproduced in full. “T rises 15 percentage points and C rises 7. The difference is 15−7=8 percentage points. Assume stable groups and unchanged measurement, no anticipation and no spillover to C. Because taking differences removes everything else, parallel trends is unnecessary and the program causes the full 8-point gain. It is significant at p<0.01. Adopt it everywhere.”

Grade and diagnosis. P's vector (4,4,4,0,0) totals 12. The first two criteria are fully earned; E3 earns its two non-trend conditions but not the missing restriction. No point is awarded for the unsupported precision or unsupported adoption sentence. Flag identification and unsupported evidence claims for critical repair. The work demonstrates a correct descriptive contrast and an invalid causal argument. The grader should ask where the p-value came from and preserve the response; the sentence alone does not establish intent or authorize a misconduct sanction.

Feedback to P. “Your two changes and their difference are correct. The sentence ‘differences removes everything else’ omits the unobserved untreated trend. Write D=τ+δ and construct the two worlds in the key to show what is missing. Withdraw the p-value unless you can supply a legitimate analysis with its data and uncertainty model; none was supplied in this exercise. Replace universal adoption with a request for evidence about adoption timing, comparison-group exposure and uncertainty. Submit a correction memo, then solve the new sensitivity task without the key.”

Complete correction memo. “T rose 55−40=15 percentage points and C rose 37−30=7; the observed contrast is D=15−7=8 percentage points. It equals the target effect only with stable populations and comparable measurement, an unaffected baseline and an untreated comparison without relevant spillovers, plus parallel untreated trends. The four rates alone cannot establish that restriction: untreated T outcomes of 47 and 55 produce different effects with the same observed table. I withdraw the significance claim because no supporting sampling or assignment analysis was supplied. Before recommending expansion, document how groups and measurements were formed, examine implementation timing and possible comparison contamination, and obtain appropriately structured data for uncertainty analysis. Earlier trends may challenge a story, but cannot prove the later counterfactual trend.” This earns full criteria if independently produced under the assignment conditions; as supplied here, it is only an illustrative correction.

Fresh reassessment. New rates are T:50→58 and C:45→49. Assume stable populations/measurement, no anticipation and an unaffected comparison. For sensitivity analysis, stipulate—not estimate—that δ lies in [−1,2] percentage points. Inputs are (50,58,45,49,-1,2). Compute the descriptive contrast and the compatible effect interval, show endpoints and write a bounded interpretation. The changes are 8 and 4, so D=4. Since τ=4−δ decreases as δ rises, τ lies in [2,5]. Values are (8,4,4,2,5). At δ=2, T's untreated post mean is 50+4+2=56 and τ=58−56=2; at δ=−1 it is 53 and τ=5. Every intermediate value is attained by an intermediate untreated mean. This is a sharp conditional identification interval within the stipulated model, not a confidence interval. Positivity depends on accepting the supplied trend-gap bound; it does not validate that bound empirically.

Fresh-task criterion guide, twenty points. Two changes 4; descriptive contrast 4; identity and bound inversion 6 (2 for τ=D−δ, 2 for lower endpoint, 2 for upper); endpoint construction 2 (1 each); interpretation 4 (2 for stipulated-bound dependence, 2 for distinguishing identification from sampling confidence). A correct interval with an unconditional causal or confidence claim leaves a critical repair unresolved. Record the actual response, assistance conditions and criterion scores before deciding whether the specific difficulty has been resolved.

5. Make the feedback usable and the decision auditable

Write feedback with an evidence location, a reason, an action and a verification task. For N, the location is the second discounted receipt; the reason is failure of reverse compounding; the action is recompute and reconcile; the verification is a new dated project. For P, the location is the causal inference; the reason is the missing untreated trend; the action is construct compatible worlds; the verification is a new bound and interpretation. “Study harder” supplies none of these. Select the obstacle that blocks the next capability rather than overwhelming the learner with every possible extension.

Fairness requires attending to the assessed capability and the conditions of access. A student's prose may be less polished while the identification argument is correct; do not deduct for elegance if it is absent from the published criteria. If communication itself is assessed, specify what the reader must be able to recover from the explanation. Consider an authorized accessible response format that preserves the intended independent reasoning and document the conditions. Do not infer that every format is equivalent, or invent institutional accommodation rules. Keep a route for questions and a stated regrading process; inspect comparable errors across the cohort, not only the most persistent complainant.

Keep separate records for the initial independent attempt, assisted correction and fresh reassessment. A proposed record is: “Task/version; criterion vector; critical flags; feedback; practice completed with assistance disclosed; fresh task/version and conditions; new evidence; next decision.” Whether a reassessment replaces a course grade is a policy decision that must be announced and reconciled with actual rules. Averaging an old misconception with a new response is not automatically the appropriate capability decision, while silently deleting the first attempt hides the learning record.

Observe what the learner actually does. A completed worksheet, a high satisfaction rating or an available answer key does not establish transfer. A remediation comparison also needs denominators: improved scores among returners can coexist with unresolved missing outcomes. Later chapters examine misconceptions and learning evidence more broadly. Here the instructor's responsibility is to make a defensible local judgment and preserve its limits.

For bounded missing outcomes, let S be the observed score total from m of N learners, with N>0. If each of the N−m missing scores can independently take any value in [L,U], the full mean lies in [(S+(N−m)L)/N,(S+(N−m)U)/N]. Every missing contribution is bounded, so summing gives the interval; filling all missing values with L or U attains the endpoints. This calculation uses the whole roster denominator. It does not establish equivalence of old and new tasks or identify an effect of instruction.

6. Exercises

  1. Adjudicate and summarize. For response N, one grader awards (2,4,3,4,2,2) and another (2,4,3,4,4,2). Resolve the disagreement using the actual response and rubric. Across a separate set of three synthetic scripts the graders' total scores are (19,12,16) and (17,12,18). Compute B, A and E as defined above. Explain why neither averaging N's grades nor B=0 settles calibration.
  2. Distinguish errors and partial credit. A new response uses 50/1.25 for both receipts and reports PVs 40,40 and NPV 16. Score only F2 and F3 under the published rubric, compare with N's subtotal for those criteria, and write one diagnostic question distinguishing a missing time concept from a transcription error.
  3. Make feedback actionable. A grader writes to K, “Wrong. Review the lecture.” Replace it with a complete feedback message and a fully specified one-period repair task using cash 45, reserve 10, cost 36 now, receipt 44 in one year, discount rate 10%, and no borrowing. Supply the full answer. Explain why simply obtaining the corrected sentence is not yet reassessment.
  4. Apply criteria fairly. A response to the original evidence task gives changes 15 and 7 percentage points, D=15−7=8 as a descriptive contrast, all E3 conditions, no justified p-value, and asks for adoption/comparison-exposure records before recommending a policy. Its prose is awkward but each claim is intelligible. A grader deducts 3 for not sounding professional. Give the defensible score under this rubric and write a complete adjudication note. State what would change if a separate, announced communication objective existed.
  5. Score versus readiness. Four equally weighted domain scores are (100,95,90,65), and an unsupported causal claim remains uncorrected. Compute the overall score and apply the proposed progression rule. Specify an actual next task using a supplied observed DID of 6 percentage points and a stipulated untreated trend gap in [−2,1]; give its answer and explain the necessary interpretation.
  6. Audit a reassessment record. Initial independently completed work earned 12/20. After reading the full key, a learner submitted a correction earning 20/20 on the same task. The instructor records “independent mastery achieved: 100%.” Write a corrected record and a complete fresh two-group task with rates T:60→63 and C:50→55. Supply its solution and the conditions under which a causal interpretation could be proposed. No sample sizes or uncertainty model are available.
  7. Bound missing remediation evidence. Eight of ten learners complete a fresh ten-point task and average 9; two results are missing in [0,10]. The original whole-group mean was 7. Bound the full fresh mean and its descriptive change from 7. Write a complete evaluation note that distinguishes outcome missingness, task comparability and a causal effect of remediation.
  8. Repair a mistaken key. A provisional one-period key says that paying 40 now for 48 in one year at 20% has NPV 8. A student submits NPV 0 with the correct denominator and challenges a deduction. Recompute, explain the boundary decision when only strictly positive-value projects are selected, and write a complete correction/regrading notice covering all affected scripts. Give one new boundary check and its answer.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

  1. N's equity dates and decomposition are correct using the carried second-receipt value. F5 earns 4, giving 19; F3 already contains the numerical deduction. Averaging 17 and 19 to 18 would contradict this rule. On the three scripts, signed differences are (2,0,−2), so B=0, A=4/3 points and E=1/3: (19,0,4/3,1/3). Zero signed difference hides offsetting disagreements, and one exact agreement out of three is only a descriptive count. Reconcile criterion evidence and retain both original vectors and the rubric version. Full credit requires the criterion-specific adjudication, all three summaries and a bounded interpretation; a statistical summary is not the adjudication itself.

  2. F2 earns 2: the first denominator is correct and the second uses one period instead of two. F3 earns 3: the first correct discounted receipt earns 1, the incorrect second earns 0, and the internally correct 40+40−64=16 earns 2. The subtotal is 5/8, compared with N's 7/8: (2,3,5,7). Ask: “If the second receipt moved from year 2 to year 3, what denominator would you use, and why?” A conceptually sound answer is 1.25³ because there are three compounding periods from now; merely saying “I copied it wrong” needs corroboration. Full credit requires these allocations, distinction between setup and evaluation, and a question that elicits the time concept. It does not require diagnosing a permanent misconception from one response.

  3. Feedback: “Your immediate cash 26 is correct, but it is below the required 30. Future receipts arrive after that check. Draw dates and mark available cash before comparing present values. Solve the following simpler case, explain the unfunded choice, then return to the two-date project with its permitted loan.” Task: “With cash 45, reserve 10, cost 36 now, certain receipt 44 in one year at 10%, and no borrowing, calculate NPV, immediate cash and the feasible choice.” Answer: PV 40, NPV 4, cash 9: (40,4,9). The project has positive value but violates the reserve; choose the outside option. Completion with feedback is practice, and a fresh independent task must test whether the timing/reserve distinction transfers. Full credit requires a usable message, complete task/answer and separation of assisted repair from reassessment.

  4. The described evidence earns (4,4,6,2,4)=20/20; the three-point style deduction is unsupported. Note: “Restore the three points because the rubric evaluates intelligible changes, identification conditions, uncertainty and a bounded recommendation, all demonstrated here. Apply the same correction to comparable scripts; retain the original and corrected record. Feedback may suggest clearer sentence structure without inventing a new scoring criterion.” If communication were an announced objective, assess its specified evidence—such as whether a reader can reconstruct the assumption chain—rather than an undefined professional voice. Full credit requires 20, criterion-based justification, consistent regrading and the stated conditional treatment of communication.

  5. The mean is (100+95+90+65)/4=87.5. It exceeds 85, but 65 is below 75 and the causal flag remains unresolved. A next task is: “For a fixed target population and clean comparison with an unaffected baseline, D=6 and δ∈[−2,1]. Derive compatible τ, construct endpoints and state what has been assumed.” Since τ=6−δ, the answer is (5,8). δ=1 gives 5 and δ=−2 gives 8; all intermediate effects are attained algebraically. This is conditional on the supplied trend restriction, not a sampling confidence interval or proof of causation from observed data alone. Full credit requires the aggregate/domain/critical decision and complete task/answer; practice followed by a separately observed independent response is still required.

  6. Corrected record: “Initial independent attempt 12/20. Same-task correction after full-key access 20/20; assisted revision completed. Independent transfer remains unobserved; no mastery decision yet.” Fresh task: “For T60→63 and C50→55, compute both changes and DID; state causal assumptions and whether a p-value can be calculated from these rates alone.” Answer: (3,5,−2) percentage points, (3,5,-2). A causal effect of−2 would require parallel untreated trends, a consistent outcome/fixed target population, an unaffected baseline and an unexposed comparison without relevant spillovers. Those assumptions are not established by the table. No justified p-value is available. Preserve the learner's actual new response and conditions; do not turn this answer guide into an observed pass. Full credit requires truthful status, changed inputs, correct signed contrast and explicit evidence boundaries.

  7. The observed total is 8×9=72. The full mean is (72+x+y)/10 with 0≤x,y≤10, so it lies in [7.2,9.2]; subtracting 7 yields [0.2,2.2]. Thus (7.2,9.2,0.2,2.2). The endpoints are attained by both missing scores 0 or both 10. Note: “Returners averaged 9, while the ten-learner fresh-task mean is only bounded by 7.2 and 9.2 under the stated score support. Even a positive descriptive change need not be learning gain: task difficulty and assistance may differ. The missing outcomes and absence of a causal comparison preclude attributing the change to remediation.” Full credit requires correct denominators, attainable bounds and all three interpretation distinctions.

  8. 48/1.2=40, so NPV 0. The key's 8 is the undiscounted cash difference. At zero value the project does not meet a strict positive-value selection rule; an indifferent-value choice would require a different stated rule. Notice: “The provisional key omitted discounting. The corrected NPV is 0. We will regrade every affected response using the corrected criterion, restore unjustified deductions and retain the old/new entries and reason. No new penalty will be introduced for relying on a misleading published key without review under the actual course policy. Independent understanding will be checked with a fresh dated task.” For example keep the payment 40 and change the year-1 receipt to 47 at 20%; NPV=−5/6, so decline. Checked values are (0,-5/6). Full credit requires the correction, strict boundary, all-script process and complete changed check; exact agreement among graders would not make the old key valid.

Teach-back and delayed retention

Teach-back. In two minutes explain why N can earn 19/20 with a wrong reported NPV while P's correct contrast does not clear a causal-reasoning flag. A complete answer identifies the original numerical slip, preserved downstream evidence, the independent identification assumption and the different next tasks. It must also say that a score, an assisted correction and an independent reassessment are different records. “Be generous with arithmetic” or “be strict with causality” is too vague; cite the criterion evidence.

Delayed task and answer. After an interval, independently assess cost 72 now and receipt 90 one year later at 25%, cash 100, reserve 30 and no borrowing. Label both dates, compute value and cash, and write feedback for a response saying “profit 18 means buy.” PV is 72, NPV 0 and cash 28: (72,0,28). The project is not strictly positive value and violates the immediate reserve. Feedback should locate the undiscounted subtraction and reserve omission, request an explicit date-zero account and reverse-compounding check, then call for a new independent task. An evaluator supplies changed numbers if this answer has already been studied. This is a proposed protocol, not evidence that retention occurred.

Sources and extension

The three official teaching-center bodies linked above were inspected for bounded advice on rubric criteria, grader discussion and feedback. Their examples and rubrics were not copied; the financial and evidence packets, point allocations and response texts are original. We have not estimated a causal effect of these practices or calibrated an institutional grading standard. Full psychometric reliability analysis, institution-specific appeals and integrity procedures, and actual learner observation require additional evidence and appropriate expertise. The next chapter applies these distinctions while leading analytical case discussion, where facilitation must preserve both participation and the quality of the reasoning.

Sources and further study

  • Carnegie Mellon Eberly Center — Grading and Performance Rubrics — Narrow professional guidance for explicit component criteria and feedback; original scoring packets constructed separately.
  • Cornell Center for Teaching Innovation — Using rubrics — Bounded recommendation to specify distinguishable performance levels and revise unclear criteria after feedback.
  • Carnegie Mellon Eberly Center — Grading and Feedback — Bounded professional advice for interpreting samples together, grading against relevant criteria and feedback explanation.
